title: The First Quarter Review: What a Fractional CFO Actually Checks When September Ends
linkedin:
Thirty September closes the first quarter of FY27. Three months of real trading data now exists against the plan most businesses set back in July.

Most owner-led businesses do nothing formal with that moment. The BAS gets lodged, the numbers get filed, and attention moves straight to October. Fair enough, that's exactly what a bookkeeper's role is built for. It isn't the same job as asking whether the business is actually tracking to plan.

Here's why the timing matters. A variance caught at three months is usually one or two decisions wide: a price that hasn't moved, a cost line that crept up with July's wage increases, a new hire not yet at the productivity the plan assumed. Fixable, without much disruption.

Leave the same gap until the half year and it's compounded through two more quarters. By nine months, in a lot of businesses, the year's outcome is effectively locked in and the conversation shifts from correction to damage control.

A proper Q1 review holds three things in view together: revenue and margin against plan, the cash conversion picture including debtor days, and whether the cost base is landing where it was expected to. None of the three is complicated alone. Missing the combination is where businesses get caught out.

The review itself isn't the valuable part. What matters is what changes for Q2 because of it, while there's still a full three quarters left to make the year's actual number look like the one that was planned.
